\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Boolean functions on the cube]
\lean{FABL.BooleanFunction}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p003-b006}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p019-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p020-b001
}
\statementsource{mossel-neeman-gaussian-noise-stability}{pdf-b53c1a5aa27d-p034-b004}
\statementsource{ghsz-combinatorial-list-decoding}{pdf-6bd33ae73ade-p005-b002}
\label{FABL.BooleanFunction}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign}
A Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube is a map from $\{ -1,1\}^n$ to
$\{\pm1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Real-valued form of a Boolean function]
\lean{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p003-b006}
\statementsource{ghsz-combinatorial-list-decoding}{pdf-6bd33ae73ade-p005-b002}
\label{FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.signValue}
For a Boolean function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{\pm1\}$, define its real-valued form by viewing
each output sign as the corresponding real number: $x\mapsto f(x)\in\mathbb R$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Uniform probability of an event]
\lean{FABL.uniformProbability}
\statementsource{lmn-constant-depth-fourier}{pdf-63759bd909d5-p003-b006}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b002}
\statementsource{ghsz-combinatorial-list-decoding}{pdf-6bd33ae73ade-p005-b002}
\label{FABL.uniformProbability}
\leanok
For a finite nonempty set $\Omega$ and a predicate $P$ on $\Omega$, define the uniform
probability of $P$ as the probability that $P(x)$ holds when $x$ is chosen uniformly
from $\Omega$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Relative Hamming distance]
\lean{FABL.relativeHammingDist}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p026-b004}
\statementsource{ghsz-combinatorial-list-decoding}{pdf-6bd33ae73ade-p005-b002}
\label{FABL.relativeHammingDist}
\leanok
For a finite nonempty set $\Omega$, a set $\beta$ with decidable equality, and functions
$f,g:\Omega\to\beta$, define their relative Hamming distance as the number of inputs on
which they differ divided by $|\Omega|$.
\end{definition}

\leanok
\uses{FABL.relativeHammingDist, FABL.uniformProbability}

\begin{definition}[Mean of a function on a finite set]
\lean{FABL.mean}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p026-b005}
\label{FABL.mean}
\leanok
For a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, define its mean as the
uniform average $\mathbb E_{x\in\Omega} f(x)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Balanced function]
\lean{FABL.IsBalanced}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p026-b005}
\label{FABL.IsBalanced}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.mean}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $f\colon\Omega\to\mathbb R$. The function $f$ is
balanced if its mean over $\Omega$ is zero.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Variance of a function]
\lean{FABL.variance}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p018-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p027-b001
}
\label{FABL.variance}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.mean}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $f\colon\Omega\to\mathbb R$. The variance of $f$ is
the mean over $\Omega$ of $(f(x)-\operatorname{mean}(f))^2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Covariance of two functions]
\lean{FABL.covariance}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p014-b004}
\label{FABL.covariance}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.mean}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $f,g\colon\Omega\to\mathbb R$. Their covariance is
the mean over $\Omega$ of $(f(x)-\operatorname{mean}(f))(g(x)-\operatorname{mean}(g))$.
\end{definition}

For a function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, its uniform inner product with itself equals
the sum of the squares of all its Fourier coefficients: $\langle
f,f\rangle=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}\widehat f(S)^2$.
\end{theorem}

Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}$ be a Boolean function, and regard its values as real
numbers. The sum, over all subsets $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$, of the squares of its
Fourier coefficients is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Squared norm equals the second moment]
\lean{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_sq_eq_expect_sq}
\label{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_sq_eq_expect_sq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformLpNorm}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$. The square of the uniform
$L^2$ norm of $f$ equals the uniform average of $f(x)^2$ over $\Omega$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform norm as a root mean square]
\lean{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_eq_sqrt_expect_sq}
\label{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_eq_sqrt_expect_sq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformLpNorm, FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_sq_eq_expect_sq}
\difficulty{4}
Let $\Omega$ be a finite set and let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$. The uniform $2$-norm of
$f$ equals the square root of the uniform expectation of $f(x)^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Squared norm and uniform inner product]
\lean{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_sq_eq_uniformInner}
\label{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_sq_eq_uniformInner}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformInner, FABL.uniformLpNorm, FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_sq_eq_expect_sq}
\difficulty{3}
For every real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, the square of its
uniform $L^2$ norm equals its uniform inner product with itself, namely the uniform
average of $f(x)^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Second moment and uniform norm]
\lean{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_eq_sqrt_uniformInner}
\label{FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_eq_sqrt_uniformInner}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.uniformInner, FABL.uniformLpNorm, FABL.uniformLpNorm_two_eq_sqrt_expect_sq}
\difficulty{3}
For every real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, its uniform $L^2$
norm equals the square root of its uniform inner product with itself.
\end{theorem}

$1-(\mathbb{E}f)^2$, and also equals four times the product of the uniform probabilities

Let $f$ be a Boolean function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube. Its variance is four
times the product of its relative Hamming distances to the constant functions $+1$ and
$-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Distance to the nearest constant function]
\lean{FABL.distanceToNearestConstant}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p027-b004}
\label{FABL.distanceToNearestConstant}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.relativeHammingDist}
For a Boolean function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, its distance to the nearest
constant function is the smaller of its relative Hamming distances from the two constant
functions with values $1$ and $-1$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{4}
Let $f,g$ be real-valued functions on the sign cube of dimension $n$. Their covariance
equals $\mathbb E[fg]-\mathbb E[f]\mathbb E[g]$, and it also equals
$\sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subseteq\{0,\ldots,n-1\}}\widehat f(S)\widehat g(S)$, where
$\widehat f(S)$ and $\widehat g(S)$ are their Fourier coefficients.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Fourier weight of a subset]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeight}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p027-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b002
}
\label{FABL.fourierWeight}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff}
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, and let $S$ be a
subset of the coordinate set $\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$. The Fourier weight of $f$ at $S$ is the
square of its Fourier coefficient at $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fourier spectral sample]
\lean{FABL.spectralSample}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p027-b008}
\label{FABL.spectralSample}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.fourierWeight, FABL.sum_sq_fourierCoeff_eq_one}
For a Boolean function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional sign cube, its Fourier spectral sample
is the probability distribution on subsets of the coordinate set that assigns each
subset $S$ probability equal to the Fourier weight of the real-valued version of $f$ at
$S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fourier weight at a fixed level]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p028-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p122-b001,

  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b002
}
\label{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierWeight}
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube and let $k$ be a
natural number. Its Fourier weight at level $k$ is the sum of the Fourier weights over
all subsets of the coordinate set having cardinality exactly $k$.
\end{definition}

\uses{FABL.fourierWeight}
Let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional sign cube and let $k$ be a
natural number. Its Fourier weight through level $k$ is the sum of the Fourier weights
over all subsets of the coordinate set having cardinality at most $k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fourier component of degree k]
\lean{FABL.degreePart}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p028-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p102-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p106-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b002
}
\label{FABL.degreePart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.monomial}
For a function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and an integer $k\ge 0$, its degree-$k$ part
is the function $x\mapsto\sum_{S\subseteq[n],\,|S|=k}\widehat f(S)\chi_S(x)$, where
$\widehat f(S)$ is the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$ and $\chi_S$ is the monomial
indexed by $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fourier weight above a degree threshold]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeightAbove}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p018-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p028-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p122-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b002
}
\label{FABL.fourierWeightAbove}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierWeight}
For a function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and an integer $k\ge 0$, define its Fourier
weight above degree $k$ to be the sum of the Fourier weights of all subsets
$S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|>k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Fourier truncation through degree k]
\lean{FABL.lowDegreePart}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p015-b014,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p028-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p102-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p106-b005,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p220-b002
}
\label{FABL.lowDegreePart}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.monomial}
For a function $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb R$ and an integer $k\ge 0$, its low-degree part
through degree $k$ is the function $x\mapsto\sum_{S\subseteq[n],\,|S|\le k}\widehat
f(S)\chi_S(x)$, where $\widehat f(S)$ is the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$ and
$\chi_S$ is the monomial indexed by $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral probability at a fixed level]
\lean{FABL.spectralSample_card_eq}
\label{FABL.spectralSample_card_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.BooleanFunction, FABL.BooleanFunction.toReal, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel, FABL.spectralSample, FABL.spectralSample_apply_toReal}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $f$ be a sign-valued function on the Boolean cube
$\{-1,1\}^n$, and let $k$ be a nonnegative integer. The probability that a spectral
sample of $f$ has exactly $k$ elements equals the sum of the squared Fourier
coefficients of the real-valued version of $f$ over all coordinate subsets of
cardinality $k$.
\end{theorem}
